So his daughters asked him; they spoke with him:

“What is this? Why did Breslov not, not find favor in your eyes?

We see that he, that he is such a servant of Hashem; he is always joyful, and he... What is this?”

He was confused; he too was confused, yes. I gave him heart trouble.

He was a great opponent, and I showed him:

“You are an opponent? Good. ‘Aishes...’—listen to the Breslov ‘Aishes Chayil.’”

He was left without hands or feet; he became nullified, yes.

He was God-fearing, and not...

He—this... he was so terribly immersed in opposition, yes, and he...

And compared with him I was nothing, a gnat, absolutely nothing, and he had heart trouble; he could find no place for himself.

He saw with his own eyes my Shabbos and his Shabbos, yes.

And how, how can one be an opponent? Yes, he had troubles; I gave him heart trouble.

His daughters, Rav Motl’s daughters, came and said to him:

“She has no Shabbos dress; a dress must be made for her.”

So Rav Motl sent me to a certain merchant who dealt in remnants—remnants, pieces, yes.

And he was—the merchant was, was selecting large pieces so that there would be enough for a dress.

So he sent me to him, and he gave me—he had merchandise that was enough for, for, for a dress, yes.

And there was a tremendous spectacle. His daughters, they, they heard the opposition,

But the Likutay Moharan and the Likutay Tfilos and the Tehillim—this made, made great troubles for them, yes.

Once Rav Shlomo came to Teveria, the Sephardic gaon, the Chacham Bashi, and he, he was old.

segments.en:
Through, through the waters of Rabbainu’s Torah, even when one falls into such a place that one thinks there is no hope whatsoever—

there is hope! I fell into water.

And this—I am telling it in words, but it is impossible to describe the moment of, of fear—

of the anguish I had when I saw that I had fallen into the pit, that I had fallen, that I was in the pit—

with nothing... no place to take hold, as...

Who can describe that moment?

And moreover, a great strengthening from this dream: “There is no despair in the world at all.”

I had already fallen into the pit and had nothing, with no hope whatsoever—and there is water!

And also what, what Rabbainu revealed.

Oy voy, oy voy, what...

what the holy Rabbainu made from simple souls, completely, completely distant from Torah, from Yiddishkait.

{These were} coarse people, who did not know the scent of Torah; they did not know.

And when they drew close to Rabbainu, there were made from them such holy tzaddikim as had never existed—

above, above nature.

This is a new matter.

And one sees Dovid HaMelech—Dovid HaMelech in Tehillim.

All of Tehillim: “Mizmor, mizmor, mizmor,” “L’Dovid mizmor,” “LaMenatzayach l’Dovid mizmor,” “mizmor.”

There is, there is “mizmor,” and there are several modes of, of, of speech.

Oy, yoy, oy, oy, oy.

Also, “Mizmor, sing to Hashem a new song”—

“a new song.”

Dovid HaMelech did not say—he said, “a new song.” He is entirely new; he is new.

“A new song”—the holy Rabbainu is “a new song”; the holy Rabbainu is this song.

And here in the Petek Rabbainu reveals a small mat... a slight thing: “Na Nach,” yes.

For sixty years I did not know of this. I only knew that it was a wonder, that it revived me, that it... yes.

Every time something fell upon me, when I fell, I took the Petek and read it, and I was—and there came about, there came about a different matter, and there came about “a new song.”

Rav Motl was also great, a great gaon in Torah.

But Rav Motl’s talents were greater than Rav Moshe Klirs’s, yes.

Because he was, he exerted himself greatly over, over, over—until he reached his level.

And Rav Motl did not need to exert himself. He only saw some matter in the Gemara or Midrash once.

He saw it only once, and he acquired it forever and ever, forever and ever, yes.

And Rav—and Rav Moshe Klirs was not, not so—his grasp was not as strong as, as Rav Motl’s.

And he knew this too.

But he, he had a famous name in Yerushalayim and throughout the world.

And I stood against him. I drew close to Rebbe Yisroel.

And he pursued me and spoke with me:

“Breslov—we, we have heard from great men, from holy tzaddikim, about Breslov.”

What? I had not heard. This, this, this is such a wondrous matter, yes.

And Rav Motl—I was a poor child, and Rav Motl, he, he was a great scholar, but he was also—

a lover of mitzvos like simple people—a mitzvah, yes.

Not like Rav... Rav Moshe Klirs—for him this mitzvah was something small, only genius and wisdom.

But Rav Motl had both; he was also a lover of mitzvos.

And he—Teveria is a small city—he knew me, and besides that, Teveria is a small city.

He... I, I found favor in his eyes. He saw me, that I was not talented.

But my truth and my heart—he loved me very much. I was in his home as in my own home, more than home; more than my own home, I came with him, prayed with him, slept at his place, and studied with him at night, yes. And he... and there was such a bond between us. But I was a simple child, and he was Rav Motl of Slonim; he was a gaon and great and wise, and wise.
